32609.etyen:
Borrowed from German Kugel (“ball, sphere; bullet”), from Middle High German kugel (“ball, sphere”). The further origin of the German word is uncertain; it may be related to Middle Dutch coghele (“ball, bullet”) and ultimately reflect Proto-West Germanic *kugulā (“ball, swelling”).
Compare Dutch kogel (“ball, sphere; bullet”), West Frisian kûgel (“bullet”), Luxembourgish Kugel (“ball, bullet”), and Danish kugle (“ball, sphere; bullet”). Also compare kula (“ball, sphere; bullet”), an inherited Old Norse word whose spherical senses were influenced by Middle Low German and German. / Inherited from Old Norse kúla (“swelling, bump”), from Proto-Germanic *kūlǭ (“lump, swelling”). The figurative senses developed through the ideas of a rounded mass, a gathered group, and a bounded occurrence or spell.
Compare Danish kule (“pit”), Swedish kula (“bump, ball”), German Kuhle (“hollow, pit”), and Dutch kuil (“pit, hole”). / Borrowed from Middle Low German kūle (“pit, hollow”), from the same Germanic word family as Old Norse kúla (“swelling, bump; hollow”) and the noun under Etymology 2.

Callisto is the second-largest of Jupiter's moons and the third-largest moon in the Solar System.

1001057.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately from Latin Callistō (“Kallisto, a nymph in Greek mythology”), from Ancient Greek Καλλιστώ (Kallistṓ, “Kallisto; the most beautiful one”), from κάλλιστος (kállistos, “most beautiful”) + -ώ (-ṓ).
The astronomical name commemorates the mythological Kallisto, a nymph associated with Zeus. The moon was discovered by Galileo Galilei in 1610 and probably almost simultaneously by Simon Marius, who proposed the name.
Parallel international forms include Danish Callisto, Swedish Callisto, German Kallisto, Dutch Callisto, Finnish Kallisto, Polish Kallisto and English Callisto
